summary: All 16 units were reviewed in full. Every numeric key, worked example and table value was recomputed independently in Python (K, G, plastic zone, size criterion, Paris closed form checked against numerical integration, Walker, FAD curve and cut-off, Basquin/Goodman/Miner, strain-life by bisection, Arrhenius, Larson-Miller with T in kelvin, ultrasonic timing, inspection intervals), and all agree with the keys within tolerance. No wrong keys or factual errors were found, and the direction of every effect (R-ratio, mean stress, strain rate, temperature, constraint) is correct. The remaining problems are minor: LaTeX left outside $...$ delimiters in plain-text fields (it will render as raw backslash text), a few over-simplified or inconsistent statements (FAD curve beyond Lr=1, Folias bulging in LBB, fail-safe terminology, root-cause framing), and some ambiguous vignette wording. This is an AI review only; the course still needs a subject-matter expert (mechanical/materials engineer) before any engineering reliance, especially for the LBB, FAD and inspection-interval material.

issues.problem: LaTeX outside math delimiters in a plain-text field: worked-example answer 'About 5.49\times10^{5} cycles (the integral was also checked numerically).' will render as raw backslash text.
issues.suggestedFix: Wrap in $...$ or write 5.49e5 / '5.49 x 10^5 cycles' in plain text. The value itself is correct (closed form 5.49e5, numerical integration 5.49e5).

issues.problem: Marking guide ('Obtains about 7.39\times10^{4} cycles') and explanation use \times outside $...$, so the number renders as raw LaTeX.
issues.suggestedFix: Wrap the numbers in $...$. The value is correct (numerical integration gives 7.39e4 cycles).

issues.problem: Mean-stress worked example has LaTeX outside math delimiters in a step ('which would be 3.62\times10^{5} cycles') and in the answer ('life about 7.05\times10^{4} cycles'); the answer also starts with a bare symbol so the sentence reads oddly.
issues.suggestedFix: Put these numbers inside $...$ delimiters. The values are correct (3.62e5 and 7.05e4).

issues.problem: Bullet says life scales as sigma_a^(1/b) 'with 1/b about -9 to -10', but the caption gives b between -0.05 and -0.12 (1/b from -8 to -20). The -9 to -10 range only holds for b about -0.1.
issues.suggestedFix: Say 'for b about -0.1, 1/b is about -10', or quote the full range of 1/b.

issues.problem: Marking guide and explanation contain LaTeX outside delimiters (e.g. '1.47\times10^{4} cycles'); several symbols/numbers do not render.
issues.suggestedFix: Wrap all numeric expressions in $...$. The values (0.00167 + 0.00172 = 0.0034 at N=1e4; life about 1.47e4 cycles) are correct.

issues.problem: Worked-example answer 'About 2.98\times10^{-11} per second' is not in math delimiters and renders as raw LaTeX.
Marking guide and explanation write '4.37\times10^{-7}' outside $...$ and the units text is broken ('s' with no exponent after unwrapped LaTeX).
issues.suggestedFix: Wrap the whole quantity '$4.37\times10^{-7}\ \text{s}^{-1}$'. Values are correct (Q about 285.5 kJ/mol; 850 K rate about 4.37e-7 s^-1).

issues.problem: Explanation has '7.466\times10^{4}' and '3.73\times10^{4}' outside math delimiters.
issues.suggestedFix: Wrap in $...$. Values are correct (74,656 cycles; half is 37,328).

issues.problem: LaTeX outside math delimiters in the worked-example answer ('1.61\times10^{4} cycles') and in the explanations/marking guides of q007, q008 and q010 (e.g. '4.66\times10^{4}', '6.157\times10^{4}', '5.38\times10^{4}').
issues.suggestedFix: Wrap every such number in $...$. All values recompute correctly (4.84e4 -> 1.61e4 cycles -> 4.03 y; 4.66e4; 8.21 y; 5.38e4 and 2.6e4).

issues.problem: The curve f = (1-0.14Lr^2)[0.3+0.7exp(-0.65Lr^6)] is the R6 Option 1 form for Lr <= 1 only (verified; the Lr,max = (sigma_y+sigma_u)/(2 sigma_y) cut-off is also correct). The table nevertheless gives f(1.2)=0.32 by extending the same expression past Lr=1. In R6 Option 1 the curve for Lr > 1 uses a different power-law branch (for the lesson's own sigma_y=350, sigma_u=480 this gives about 0.20 at Lr=1.2, so 0.32 is non-conservative). The row also lies beyond the worked example's Lr,max of 1.19. Also 'Lr -> 1 means plastic collapse' ignores that collapse is at Lr,max.
issues.suggestedFix: State that the expression applies for Lr <= 1 (the table row at 1.2 should be removed, or flagged as beyond the stated validity for this teaching curve with a note that the governing procedure uses a different branch above Lr=1). Recommend a source check against R6/BS 7910.

issues.problem: Worked example calls a W = 200 mm plate with a 40 mm central crack a 'wide plate' and takes Y = 1, while also using a finite-width net-section reference stress. The secant factor for 2a/W = 0.2 is Y = 1.026, so K is about 2.6 percent low.
issues.suggestedFix: Either increase W or say 'take Y = 1 for simplicity (the secant factor would be 1.026)'. The conclusion (point inside the curve at 150 MPa, outside at 270 MPa) is unchanged.

issues.problem: Caption says ignoring shell bulging with Y = 1 is 'mildly unconservative'. For the first worked example (r = 0.5 m, t = 20 mm, a = 141 mm) the Folias factor is about 1.85 and the critical half-length falls from 141 mm to about 79 mm (roughly 44 percent smaller), which is not mild. LBB is still met in that example (79 mm > 40 mm), so the conclusion survives, and the second example (19.9 mm vs about 18.6 mm) is only slightly affected. The lesson also mixes 'critical length larger than the wall thickness' with a half-length criterion a_c >= 2t.
issues.suggestedFix: Say 'unconservative, increasingly so for long cracks in thin-walled shells (Folias factor), so real assessments must apply a bulging correction'. Clarify that a_c is a half-length and that a_c >= 2t means a full critical length of at least 4t.

issues.problem: The unit uses 'fail-safe design' for tolerating a crack of detectable size (critical crack length), whereas the leak-before-break unit defines fail-safe as redundant load paths after a member failure and uses 'damage tolerance' for flaw-growth-based design.
issues.suggestedFix: Use 'damage-tolerant' (or 'flaw-tolerant') in this unit, or add a note that the term is used loosely here, so it matches the definitions in fitness-for-service.

issues.problem: The lesson defines root cause by a counterfactual test, then labels the Liberty-ship low-toughness steel as the root cause and weld defects, sharp hatch corners and residual stress as merely contributing. Removing any of those factors would also plausibly have prevented the brittle fractures, so it fails the lesson's own test. 'Real failures usually have a single root cause' is also an overstatement. The Comet description (window and rivet-hole corners, pressurisation fatigue) is accurate in outline but is stated without hedging (the initiating cracks were at the ADF aerial window cut-outs).
issues.suggestedFix: Say failures often have more than one necessary cause and that the 'root cause' is the one chosen for corrective action. Use hedged wording for the Comet (for example 'cracks initiated at corners of cut-outs and rivet holes') and mention that Liberty-ship fractures needed both a notch-brittle steel and stress concentrations or flaws.

issues.problem: Explanation states 'At the rated loading the weld toe still creates the crack' but the vignette gives no evidence that the bracket would have failed at rated load; the counterfactual is asserted rather than shown.
issues.suggestedFix: Add to the vignette that the unground weld toe class is known to crack at rated load (or that a ground-toe bracket under the same overload survived), or reword the explanation as the 'most reasonable' judgement.

issues.problem: Case (iii) 'in-plane shear parallel to the crack plane' does not say how the shear is oriented relative to the crack front, so it could be Mode II (shear perpendicular to the front) or Mode III (parallel to the front). Case (ii) 'keyed shaft end' is also an odd example for a circumferential crack front.
issues.suggestedFix: Specify 'shear acting parallel to the crack plane and perpendicular to the crack front' in (iii), and describe (ii) simply as a circumferentially cracked round shaft in torsion.

issues.problem: Table gives 'Surface half-penny crack (typical, shallow)' with Y about 0.7. About 0.66-0.71 is the free-surface value at the deepest point of a semicircular (a/c = 1) surface crack; a shallow, long semi-elliptical surface crack tends towards about 1.12. 'Shallow' is therefore misleading. (Unverified against a handbook; recommend a source check.)
issues.suggestedFix: Label it 'semicircular surface crack (a/c = 1), deepest point, Y about 0.71' and note Y rises towards about 1.12 for long shallow surface cracks.
